name: tarroo-ushtey

attributes.attribute: water bull of the Isle of Man
blighted crops rather than eating people
also spelled theroo ushta and classed as a malevolent bull of Manx tradition
a clear adaptation of the tarbh uisge from Scottish Gaelic tradition
frequents swamps and shallow water and at times walks the fields beside farm cattle
judged less malign than the cabyll-ushtey of the same island

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The tarroo-ushtey stands as the water bull of the Isle of Man. This creature is far less fierce than most water beasts. Other monsters of the deep ate people and cattle. The tarroo-ushtey only ruined the farmers' crops. Manx tradition sets it apart from the worst of the water animals. A wand of rowan would turn it away. The dictionary also gives the spelling theroo ushta. It notes the creature is a malevolent bull of Manx lore. Its form derives clearly from the tarbh uisge. The tarbh uisge is a figure of Scottish Gaelic tradition. Among its habits, the beast frequents swamps and shallow water. At times it walks the open fields beside the farmer's cattle. Even with that reach, the tarroo-ushtey is less malign than the cabyll-ushtey. The cabyll-ushtey is the water horse of the same island.

okr.objective: Fuse the baseline Manx water-bull story with the article's tarbh uisge derivation, habitat, and cabyll-ushtey comparison.
key_results: Identifies the tarroo-ushtey as the Manx water bull that ruined crops but did not eat people
Notes the secondary spelling theroo ushta and the malevolent Manx bull label
Derives the figure from the Scottish Gaelic tarbh uisge
Places it in swamps and shallow water and in the open farm fields
Marks the tarroo-ushtey as less malign than the cabyll-ushtey
Keeps the rowan-wand charm from the baseline
